days.task: Rewrite one vague request into a full brief
days.why: Specific context (audience, goal, length, format) is the single biggest lever on output quality.
steps: Pick a real request you made this week, like "help me with this deck".
Rewrite it: who it's for, what decision it supports, length, format, what to avoid.
Run both versions and note three differences in the answers.

days.task: Teach Claude your house style with one example
days.why: An example of output you liked transfers tone and structure faster than any description.
steps: Paste a past email or proposal section you're proud of.
Ask for a new one on a different topic in the same style.
Note what carried over and what didn't.

days.task: Make Claude reason before it answers
days.why: Asking for step-by-step reasoning and stated assumptions catches errors in scope and pricing logic.
steps: Pick a trade-off you're weighing, such as two solution options or two commercial models.
Ask Claude to think it through step by step, then list every assumption it made.
Challenge the weakest assumption and see how the answer changes.

days.task: Replace "make it better" with three precise edits
days.why: Targeted revision requests converge in one round instead of five.
steps: Take any draft Claude wrote for you.
Give exactly three changes: tone, one thing to add, one thing to cut.
Compare against a plain "improve this" request.

days.task: Rehearse a tough customer meeting with role-play
days.why: Having Claude play a sceptical CTO surfaces objections before the real meeting does.
steps: Describe the proposal and the customer's priorities, with no confidential names.
Ask Claude to play the CTO and raise its three hardest objections.
Draft your answers, then ask it to rate them as the CTO.

days.task: Set up a project for one recurring workstream
days.why: Projects keep reference docs and instructions in one place, so you stop re-explaining context.
steps: Create a project for one ongoing bid or account.
Add two or three reference documents and short custom instructions.
Ask one question that needs those documents to answer.

days.task: Interrogate a long document with citations
days.why: Requiring section or clause references makes answers checkable, which matters for contracts and RFPs.
steps: Attach an RFP, SOW or contract.
Ask five questions and require a section or clause number for each answer.
Spot-check two citations against the document.

days.task: Turn an RFP section into a compliance matrix
days.why: Structured output (tables with fixed columns) turns reading time into a usable work product.
steps: Pick one RFP section.
Ask for a table: requirement, compliance status, response summary, owner.
Ask Claude to flag any requirement it was unsure how to classify.

days.task: Build an English–Chinese terminology glossary
days.why: A shared glossary keeps customer-facing English and internal Chinese material consistent.
steps: Draft a short English summary of a solution.
Ask for the Chinese version plus a glossary of every technical term used.
Save the glossary and reuse it in your next bilingual task.

days.task: Start your personal prompt library
days.why: Five prompts you trust are worth more than fifty you half-remember.
steps: Look back over this fortnight's best prompts.
Save five as reusable templates, with blanks for the parts that change.
Name each one by the job it does.

days.task: Write your first skill for a task you repeat
days.why: A skill packages instructions Claude follows every time, like a checklist it never forgets.
steps: Pick a task you do weekly, such as a proposal QA pass.
Write the steps and quality bar as if briefing a new colleague.
Ask Claude to turn that into a skill and test it on one real file.

days.task: Let a connector do the reading for you
days.why: Connected apps let Claude pull context from mail or notes instead of you pasting it.
steps: Connect one app you use daily, like Gmail or Notion.
Ask for a summary of this week's threads on one topic, with what's waiting on you.
Check one item against the source.

days.task: Schedule a weekly digest
days.why: Scheduled tasks turn a good prompt into something that runs without you remembering it.
steps: Choose a weekly summary you'd actually read.
Ask Claude to set it up as a scheduled task.
Review the first run and tighten the prompt.

days.task: Have Claude build a checking spreadsheet
days.why: Formulas that cross-check totals and quantities catch the errors that slip through manual review.
steps: Describe a pricing sheet or bill of quantities you maintain.
Ask for an .xlsx with check formulas: totals tie out, no blank unit prices, margins in range.
Break one value on purpose and confirm a check catches it.

days.task: Spec one chore for full automation
days.why: Writing the spec first (inputs, steps, output, checks) is what makes an automation reliable.
steps: Pick the presales chore that eats the most of your week.
Write: trigger, inputs, steps, output, how you'd know it's right.
Ask Claude what's missing from the spec.

days.task: Study this app's morning refresh as a case study
days.why: It's a full loop: a scheduled prompt, web research, a data file, and an app that reads it.
steps: Ask Claude to show you the scheduled task prompt and data/market.json.
Trace how a number gets from a web source to your screen.
Suggest one improvement and have Claude make it.

days.task: Write a script that QA-checks a slide deck
days.why: Programmatic checks find leftover placeholders, wrong fonts and missing page numbers in seconds.
steps: Give Claude a sample .pptx and list five things you always check.
Have it write a Python script that reports each issue by slide.
Run it on a real deck and review the report.

days.task: Turn the script into a reusable tool
days.why: A tool you can hand any deck to is worth more than a one-off script.
steps: Ask Claude to package the checker as a skill or small command.
Add a clear pass/fail summary at the top of its output.
Test it on two different decks.

days.task: Run a multi-step task with research, draft and review
days.why: Splitting work into stages, with a separate check at the end, is the core pattern behind agents.
steps: Pick a market or technology question for a customer brief.
Ask Claude to research it, draft a one-page brief, then review its own draft against the sources.
Compare the reviewed version with the first draft.

days.task: Ship it and plan what's next
days.why: Showing a colleague what you built makes the learning stick and surfaces the next idea.
steps: Demo your deck checker or automation to one colleague.
Write down what they'd want it to do next.
Tell Claude, and ask for your next four weeks of lessons.
